Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current state-of-the-art self-explainable neural networks, particularly Prototypical Part Networks (ProtoPNets), suffer from a critical limitation in their interpretability: **semantic redundancy**. While these models aim to mimic human reasoning by matching input regions to learned "part prototypes," the learned prototypes often collapse into repetitive concepts (e.g., multiple prototypes identifying the same visual texture or region). Consequently, the resulting explanations are non-comprehensive, failing to cover the diverse set of semantic parts (such as head, torso, and legs) required for a holistic and transparent decision-making process. Existing methods utilizing parametric learning with regularization have struggled to enforce sufficient diversity among these prototypes.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can overcome semantic redundancy by shifting from parametric prototype learning to a **non-parametric, clustering-based approach**.

Our intuition is that foundation vision models (e.g., self-supervised Vision Transformers) already encode robust, semantic object parts in their latent space. Instead of learning prototypes via gradient descent from scratch, we propose to discover them by partitioning the deep feature space into semantically distinct clusters. By enforcing constraints that require unique assignments between image patches and prototypes, we expect to force the model to discover a diverse, comprehensive set of object parts, thereby significantly improving the quality and distinctiveness of the generated visual explanations.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a two-stage framework designed to disentangle prototype discovery from feature space adaptation.

**Stage 1: Non-parametric Prototype Discovery**
We will leverage a frozen, pre-trained Vision Transformer backbone to extract feature patches. Rather than training prototypes as weights, we will derive them effectively via **constrained clustering**:
*   **Optimal Transport Formulation:** We will treat the assignment of feature patches to prototypes as an optimal transport problem. We intend to apply strict "equipartition" constraints. This ensures that every prototype represents a distinct cluster of features and prevents the trivial solution where a single dominant feature activates multiple prototypes.
*   **Momentum Updates:** Prototypes will be updated as the empirical mean of the feature patches assigned to their specific cluster. This ensures the prototype represents the "average" visual concept of that specific part across the dataset.

**Stage 2: Prototype-Anchored Feature Refinement**
Once diverse prototypes are discovered, we will freeze them and adapt the backbone to the target domain to optimize classification performance without losing semantic structure:
*   **Block Expansion:** To avoid catastrophic forgetting or destroying the pre-trained latent structure, we will insert lightweight, trainable identity blocks into the backbone while freezing the original weights.
*   **Patch-Prototype Grounding:** We will employ a contrastive-style objective that acts as a "magnetic" force. It will pull image patches closer to their assigned prototype in the embedding space and push them away from other prototypes within the same class. This sharpens the decision boundaries and ensures feature locality.

**Inference Mechanism**
The final classification will remain interpretable: similarity maps between the input image and the learned prototypes will be generated. The final class prediction will be a weighted average of these similarity scores, allowing us to trace the decision back to specific, non-overlapping visual parts.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Elimination of Redundancy:** A theoretical framework that guarantees diverse visual explanations by solving the prototype collapse problem inherent in standard ProtoPNets.
2.  **Unsupervised Part Discovery:** A method to extract semantic object parts from foundation models without requiring part-level annotations (bounding boxes or masks).
3.  **Enhanced Interpretability Metrics:** We aim to formalize the evaluation of explanations by introducing concepts of "Distinctiveness" (how unique each prototype is) and "Comprehensiveness" (how much of the object is covered by the explanation), moving beyond simple accuracy-based metrics.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed and executed a comprehensive evaluation framework to assess the performance of a proposed non-parametric part prototype learning method for interpretable image classification.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **CUB-200-2011:** 11,788 images spanning 200 bird species.
    *   **Stanford Cars:** 16,185 images from 196 car models.
    *   **Stanford Dogs:** 20,580 images from 120 breeds.
    *   *Note:* The primary quantitative benchmark focused on CUB-200-2011.

*   **Backbone Models (Foundation Models):**
    *   **DINOv2 ViT-B/14:** Latest checkpoint, trained on LVD-142M.
    *   **DINOv2 ViT-S/14:** Latest checkpoint, trained on LVD-142M.
    *   **DINO ViT-B/16:** Original DINO trained on ImageNet.
    *   *Configuration:* Models were used as feature extractors and then fine-tuned.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **ProtoPNet** (Standard Prototypical Part Network)
    *   **Deformable ProtoPNet**
    *   **ProtoPool**
    *   **TesNet**
    *   **EvalProtoPNet**
    *   **Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs):** Vanilla CBM, CBM-h (with residual fitting), CEM, and Huang et al. (specifically for the concept learning experiment).

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Class.:** Top-1 Classification Accuracy (%).
    *   **Con.:** Consistency Score (%) - evaluates if a prototype corresponds to the same object part across different images.
    *   **Sta.:** Stability Score (%) - measures if a prototype corresponds to the same part under noise perturbation.
    *   **Dis.:** Distinctiveness Score (%) - **[New Metric]** quantifies the overlap among object parts learned by prototypes within the same class (higher is better).
    *   **Comprehensiveness Score:** **[New Metric]** measures the coverage of the object foreground by the prototypes (higher is better).
    *   **Loc.:** Concept Trustworthiness (%) - used specifically for CBM comparisons.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Prototypes per Class ($K$):** Evaluated at $K=3$ and $K=5$.
    *   **Supervision:** Image-level class labels only.
    *   **Training Stage 1 (Prototype Discovery):**
        *   Epochs: 1.
        *   Clustering momentum coefficient ($\beta$): 0.99.
        *   Entropic regularization ($\kappa$): 0.05.
    *   **Training Stage 2 (Feature Refinement):**
        *   Epochs: 5.
        *   Patch-Prototype Contrastive Loss weight ($\lambda_{PPC}$): 0.8.
        *   Block Expansion ($m$): 1 added ViT block.
    *   **Optimization:**
        *   Optimizer: Adam.
        *   Backbone Learning Rate: 0.0001 (1e-4).
        *   Modulation Vector ($w$) Learning Rate: 0.000001 (1e-6).
    *   **Baseline Configuration:** Previous ProtoPNet architectures were trained with $m=3$ (block expansion) as it produced the best historical results.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Training and Stability:**
*   We observed that the proposed method outperformed previous methods in classification accuracy by margins of 0.16% and 2.39% when trained with revised DINOv2 and DINO ViT-B backbones, respectively.
*   While Consistency scores were similar to state-of-the-art, Stability scores were higher in most settings.
*   The most significant quantitative improvement was observed in Distinctiveness, surpassing previous methods by margins of 4.83%, 3.49%, and 8.93% when setting 5 prototypes per class.
*   During ablation, removing unique-assignment and equipartition constraints caused the model to fail in grouping semantically similar patch tokens, rendering the prototypes incapable of classification (accuracy dropped to 9.25%).
*   Removing foreground extraction significantly decreased prototype quality as background tokens were included in the learning process.

**Visual Prototype Analysis:**
*   **Vanilla ProtoPNet:** Activation maps revealed poor interpretability. The most activated areas were frequently outside the foreground object, scattered across the background. The network frequently performed classification by comparing latent image patches with mostly the same object part (low diversity).
*   **ProtoPool:** Learned prototypes attended to various areas within the object, but we still observed explanations highlighting background regions.
*   **EvalProtoPNet:** Produced better visual explanations than vanilla ProtoPNet and ProtoPool, with prototypes attending to different object parts. However, we observed a lack of diversity; often multiple activation maps highlighted the same concept (e.g., at least two out of four maps highlighted the same region). This held true for both ViT and CNN backbones.
*   **Our Method:** Prototypes successfully captured semantically distinct parts of the object (e.g., distinguishing between the head, wing, tail, and legs of a bird) within a single sample. This resulted in the most conceptually diverse set of explanations among all compared methods.

**Comprehensiveness and Distinctiveness:**
*   Analysis of Distinctiveness across varying bounding box sizes showed that our framework consistently yielded higher scores, indicating less overlap between explanations.
*   Analysis of Comprehensiveness across varying thresholds showed that while original ProtoPNet failed to cover multiple parts of the object, our framework recognized concepts that provided broader coverage of the object foreground.

**Concept Learning Adaptation:**
*   When adapting the prototypes to produce trustworthy concept-based explanations, we found that naive Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) on ViT backbones failed to produce trustworthy explanations despite high accuracy.
*   Our method yielded trustworthiness scores comparable to specialized methods (Huang et al.) while achieving higher classification performance.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Classifying images with an interpretable decision-making process is a critical challenge in computer vision. While Prototypical Part Networks (ProtoPNets) have emerged as a leading approach for self-explainable neural networks by matching input regions to learned "prototypes," current implementations suffer from a significant theoretical limitation: **redundancy**. We observe that multiple prototypes within the same class often converge to the same semantic region (e.g., three prototypes all attending to a bird's wing), leaving other distinctive parts (legs, tail) unrepresented.

This phenomenon stems from the standard parametric training of prototypes, where learning is guided by weak regularizations that fail to enforce semantic diversity. Consequently, the resulting explanations are non-comprehensive and repetitive, undermining the goal of transparent, human-like visual reasoning. There is currently no robust mechanism to ensure that the set of learned prototypes for a category covers a holistic and mutually exclusive set of semantic concepts.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose to fundamentally alter the prototype acquisition process by shifting from parametric optimization to **Non-parametric Part Prototype Learning**.

Our hypothesis is that by treating prototype discovery as a **feature clustering problem** within the robust semantic space of foundation models (specifically self-supervised Vision Transformers like DINO-ViTs), we can enforce semantic distinctiveness. We posit that formulating the assignment of image patches to prototypes as an **Optimal Transport (OT)** problem with equipartition constraints will force the model to discover diverse, non-overlapping concepts. Furthermore, we hypothesize that a two-stage training regime—first discovering prototypes via clustering, then refining the backbone via a novel "Block Expansion" technique—will allow us to adapt foundation models to specific domains without degrading their pre-trained semantic structure.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a framework consisting of two distinct training stages: (1) Non-parametric Prototype Discovery and (2) Prototype-Anchored Feature Space Tuning.

### 1. Architecture and Inference Logic
We will define the model using a Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone $\mathcal{F}$. The core interpretable component is the prototype tensor $\mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times K \times D}$, where $C$ is the number of classes, $K$ is the number of prototypes per class, and $D$ is the embedding dimension.

Given an input image $\mathbf{X}$, the backbone produces patch tokens $\mathbf{f} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{X}) \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times w \times D}$. We calculate similarity maps $\mathbf{S}$ between tokens and prototypes. The final class logit is a weighted average of the maximum activation scores of the prototypes associated with class $c$:
$$ \mathrm{logit}^c = \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k^c \cdot g_k^c $$
where $g_k^c = \max_{\tilde{\mathbf{f}} \in \mathbf{f}} \mathrm{Sim}(\tilde{\mathbf{f}}, \mathbf{P}_k^c)$ represents the maximum presence of prototype $k$, and $w$ is a learned modulation vector.

### 2. Stage I: Non-parametric Prototype Learning via Optimal Transport
In this stage, the backbone is frozen. We treat the batch of latent patch tokens as a bag of features. To ensure prototypes represent distinct parts, we formulate the assignment of foreground patches to prototypes as an Optimal Transport problem.

Let $\mathbf{f}^c$ denote $N$ foreground patches belonging to class $c$. We compute a similarity matrix $\mathbf{S}^c \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}$ between these patches and the class prototypes. We seek an assignment matrix $\mathbf{A}^c \in \{0, 1\}^{N \times K}$ that maximizes similarity subject to equipartition constraints (ensuring every prototype is used equally):

$$ \operatorname*{max}_{\mathbf{A}^c \in \mathcal{A}^c} \operatorname{Tr} \left( (\mathbf{A}^c)^\top \mathbf{S}^c \right) + \kappa h(\mathbf{A}^c) $$

Here, $\kappa h(\mathbf{A}^c)$ is an entropic regularization term to smooth the solution. The constraints are defined as:
$$ (\mathbf{A}^c)^\top \mathbf{1}_N = \frac{1}{K} \mathbf{1}_K, \quad \mathbf{A}^c \mathbf{1}_K = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{1}_N $$

We will solve this efficiently using the **Sinkhorn-Knopp Algorithm**:
$$ \mathbf{A}^{c, *} = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{u}) \exp\left( \frac{\mathbf{S}^c}{\kappa} \right) \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{v}) $$

**Momentum Update:** Once the assignment $\mathbf{A}^{c, *}$ is determined, we update the prototypes non-parametrically as the moving average of the patch features assigned to them. This ensures the prototype represents the empirical mean of the cluster:
$$ \mathbf{P}_k^c \gets \mathbf{P}_k^c + (1 - \beta) \overline{\mathbf{f}}^{c,k} $$
where $\beta$ controls the update speed and $\overline{\mathbf{f}}^{c,k}$ is the mean feature of patches assigned to prototype $k$.

### 3. Stage II: Prototype-Anchored Feature Space Tuning
After discovering prototypes, we must adapt the backbone to the target domain without destroying the semantic layout. We propose **Block Expansion**: we divide the ViT blocks into groups and insert a trainable identity block $\mathcal{F}_{id}$ at the end of each group. We freeze the original backbone weights and prototypes, training only the $\mathcal{F}_{id}$ blocks and the modulation vector $w$.

To improve feature locality, we introduce an **In-class Patch-Prototype Contrastive Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPC}}$)**. This loss pulls a patch towards its assigned prototype and pushes it away from other prototypes *within the same class*:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPC}} = \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}} \frac{\exp((\mathbf{f}_i^c)^\top \mathbf{P}_{k_i}^c)}{\exp((\mathbf{f}_i^c)^\top \mathbf{P}_{k_i}^c) + \sum_{\mathbf{P}_{k_j}^c \in \mathcal{P}^{c-}} \exp((\mathbf{f}_i^c)^\top \mathbf{P}_{k_j}^c)} $$

The total training objective for Stage II will be:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ce}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{PPC}} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPC}} $$

### 4. Proposed Evaluation Metrics
To rigorously verify our hypothesis regarding diversity, we will define two new metrics:

1.  **Distinctiveness Score:** Quantifies the overlap between regions activated by different prototypes of the same class. Lower overlap implies higher distinctiveness.
    $$ O(x) = \frac{1}{K(K-1)/2} \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \sum_{l=k+1}^{K} \mathrm{IoU}(R^{c_x, k}(x), R^{c_x, l}(x)) $$
2.  **Comprehensiveness Score:** Measures how thoroughly the union of all prototype activations covers the ground truth foreground object mask $M_x$.
    $$ \text{Score} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}|} \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \mathrm{IoU}\left(M_x, \bigcup_{k=1}^{K} \hat{M}^{c_x, k}(x)\right) $$

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Framework Novelty:** We will present the first ProtoPNet architecture that utilizes non-parametric prototype learning via Optimal Transport to guarantee semantically distinct object parts.
2.  **Theoretical Advancement:** By decoupling prototype discovery (clustering) from classification tuning (Block Expansion), we effectively leverage the robust semantics of foundation models (DINO) for interpretable tasks, avoiding the catastrophic forgetting often seen in fine-tuning.
3.  **Methodological Rigor:** The introduction of the Distinctiveness and Comprehensiveness Scores will provide the field with a standard quantitative framework to assess the diversity of visual explanations, moving beyond qualitative visual inspection.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

network.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
network.web_access: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

tools.permissions: upstream's own agent settings; provider web search denied by managed settings (Claude Code permissions.deny WebSearch, Codex web_search="disabled")

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no coding agent: a 23-stage prompt-chain pipeline over the Anthropic Messages API

network.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).

tools.permissions: no tool calls (requests carry model, messages, max_tokens); generated experiments run as plain subprocesses in the container

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
